extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness (35 U.S.C. §103) — when and how to find a claim obvious based on prior art, including rationales such as substitution, analogous art, lead compound selection, predictability, and the use/treatment of secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a reference is reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed by the invention; a reference in a different field may be analogous art if it addresses a similar problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the problem to be solved — if the reference and the application both address the same or a similar problem, the reference may be analogous art even if in a different field (ICON: Teague addressed retaining folding mechanisms generally; thus it was analogous to a treadmill application). Be aware that a reference may be narrowly drawn and thereby restricted in usefulness, but addressing a similar problem 'goes a long way' toward demonstrating a reason to combine references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference only teaches away if it teaches that the combination or modification is undesirable or would not work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference does not teach that a combination is undesirable, it cannot be said to teach away. In assessing inoperability or dissuasive teaching, do not 'ignore the modifications that one skilled in the art would make to a device borrowed from the prior art' (ICON). A finding that a reference 'at most teaches away' is not dispositive if the reference also instructs that the known approach achieves the desired function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution / predictable result
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting a known element for another or applying a known technique to prior art is obvious when it yields predictable results and the function of the substituted element is well known in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Agrizap, Gregory/Fuller scenarios): when prior art shows differing load-bearing members or differing attachment means, substituting one known element for another to transfer load is an obvious, predictable substitution. The Federal Circuit described such situations as 'textbook case[s] of... familiar elements according to known methods that does no more than yield predictable results.' Objective evidence of nonobviousness must specifically address this predictability to overcome an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine (KSR flexible approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reason or motivation to combine prior art references is required, but it need not be an explicit teaching or a rigid TSM (teaching-suggestion-motivation) showing; the requisite motivation can come from many sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require an explicit teaching in the prior art to isolate or modify components (Aventis, Eisai). It is sufficient to show that the claimed and prior art compounds have a 'sufficiently close relationship... to create an expectation' that the new compound will have similar properties. The motivation may be implicit in the totality of the prior art or in the nature of the problem to be solved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead compound selection (chemical cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness based on structural similarity requires identification of some motivation that would have led a person of ordinary skill to select and modify a known compound (a 'lead compound') to achieve the claimed compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'lead compound' concept may be applied flexibly — any known compound might serve as a lead compound for obviousness purposes (Eisai). Structural similarity can supply the reason to modify; an expectation of similar properties (in light of the totality of the prior art) can be sufficient even without an explicit prior-art teaching. A lead compound used for obviousness need not be one pharmaceutical chemists would pick for development (e.g., could be inactive) but there still must be some reason to start with it beyond mere existence (Altana, Altana/Teva; Altana/compound 12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to modify and reasonable expectation of success (chemistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness of a claimed chemical compound, there must be both a reason to modify a prior art compound and a reasonable expectation of success in making the claimed compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procter & Gamble v. Teva: even if a prior-art compound is presumed an appropriate lead, there must be evidence that the modifications would have been routine and that one of ordinary skill would have expected success. Lack of routine modifications or reasonable expectation of success supports nonobviousness. Unexpected results (e.g., superior potency, lower toxicity) can rebut a prima facie obviousness showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations / objective indicia
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider objective evidence of nonobviousness (skepticism by experts, copying, praise, commercial success, long-felt but unsolved need) as potential rebuttal to a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence must have a nexus to the claimed invention (coextensive with the claims) to carry weight (Muniauction: lack of nexus means evidence not entitled to substantial weight). Evaluate commercial success and long-felt need as of the filing date (P&G: long-felt need evaluated as of filing date). Weight of commercial success may be reduced if the competing product is owned by the same assignee as the patentee. Credibility of witnesses and test data showing unexpected superior properties increase probative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Known Technique To Improve Similar Devices — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim under the rationale that a known technique was used to improve similar devices, the examiner must make specified factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device upon which the claimed invention is an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a 'comparable' device that has been improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have applied the known 'improvement' technique in the same way to the 'base' device and that the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham factual findings necessary to explain the conclusion of obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, the rationale cannot be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a Known Technique to a Known Device Ready for Improvement — required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting based on applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement, the examiner must make specified factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device upon which the claimed invention can be seen as an 'improvement'; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a known technique applicable to the base device; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and resulted in an improved system; and (4) whatever additional Graham factual findings are necessary given the facts of the case. The rationale rests on the technique being part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and the skill of the ordinary artisan
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness rationales depending on known techniques assume the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill; if application would have been beyond that skill, the claim is not obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR cautions that if the actual application of the technique would have been beyond the skill of one of ordinary skill in the art, then using the technique would not have been obvious. Always tie predictability findings back to Graham factual inquiries; include any additional facts necessary to explain the conclusion of obviousness. 'If any of these findings cannot be made, then this rationale cannot be used to support a conclusion that the claim would have been obvious.'
